slides: Welcome back. Today we're learning about polygons. A polygon question shows up in most exams. Most of these questions use the same few rules, and we'll learn all of them today.

slides.say: A polygon is a closed shape with straight sides. It has three sides or more. We already know two polygons. A triangle is a polygon with three sides. A quadrilateral is a polygon with four sides.
Five sides is a pentagon. Six sides is a hexagon. Seven sides is a heptagon. And eight sides is an octagon.
Look at these shapes. Their sides are not equal, and their angles are not equal. They're still a pentagon, a hexagon, a heptagon and an octagon. The name only tells us how many sides there are.

Now the angles. In a triangle, the angles add up to one hundred eighty. In a quadrilateral, they add up to three hundred sixty. So the sum of the angles depends on the number of sides. The more sides, the bigger the sum.
Here's the rule. The sum of the angles is one hundred eighty, times the bracket, n minus two. n is the number of sides.
at: n is the number of sides

slides.say: Let's check it on a quadrilateral first, because we know its sum. n is four. Four minus two is two. Two times one hundred eighty is three hundred sixty. That's exactly the sum we know.
Now a pentagon. n is five. Five minus two is three. Three times one hundred eighty is five hundred forty. So the five angles of any pentagon add up to five hundred forty.
at: the five angles of any pentagon

slides.say: And a hexagon. n is six. Six minus two is four. Four times one hundred eighty is seven hundred twenty.

Where does this rule come from? Let's take a pentagon and pick one corner. From that corner, we draw lines to the other corners. A line that joins two corners that are not next to each other is called a diagonal.

The diagonals cut the pentagon into triangles. One, two, three triangles. Each triangle has one hundred eighty degrees inside it. So the pentagon has three times one hundred eighty, which is five hundred forty. That's the same as the rule.

Now a heptagon, with seven sides. From one corner we get one, two, three, four, five triangles. Five times one hundred is five hundred, and five times eighty is four hundred. Together, nine hundred. So the angles of a heptagon add up to nine hundred.
Why n minus two? Every triangle sits on one side of the polygon. But the two sides that touch our corner don't get a triangle of their own. So n sides give n minus two triangles.
at: the two sides that touch our corner

slides: So if you forget the rule in the exam, that's fine. Split the polygon into triangles from one corner, and count them.

slides.say: Now let's see what happens when we add a side. Here's a pentagon. I erase this side, and I draw two new sides instead. Now there are six sides.
What really changed? We added one more triangle. One more triangle is one more one hundred eighty. So every extra side adds one hundred eighty to the sum.
So the sums go up in steps of one hundred eighty. A pentagon, five hundred forty. A hexagon, seven hundred twenty. A heptagon, nine hundred. And an octagon, one thousand eighty.

This helps a lot when a question compares two polygons. Say one polygon has twelve sides, and another has nine. What's the difference between their angle sums? The first one has three more sides. Each side adds one hundred eighty. So the difference is three times one hundred eighty, which is five hundred forty.
at: The first one has three more sides

slides.say: Sometimes we know the sum, and we need the number of sides. Say the angles add up to nine hundred. How many sides are there?
at: Say the angles add up to nine hundred

slides.say: Every triangle is one hundred eighty. Nine hundred divided by one hundred eighty is five, because five times one hundred eighty is nine hundred. So there are five triangles.
at: Every triangle is one hundred eighty

slides.say: Careful here. Five is the number of triangles, not the number of sides. There are always two more sides than triangles. So there are five plus two, seven sides. It's a heptagon, like before. [pause] Okay. I'll see you in the next part.
at: So there are five plus two
